prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the layout of an outdoor sports field across the five frames as the camera wearer pitches their head from looking up at the sky (frame 1), forward across the grass toward a distant treeline and light poles roughly 40–80 m away (frames 2–3), straight down at the ground within 0.5–1.5 m and arm's reach (frame 4), and back up to the sky with distant trees in the lower corners (frame 5). In frame 1, the airborne ball in the upper center appears as a distinct medium-grey disc (~3–8 m away and above the wearer) against the black sky, isolating its foreground depth much more clearly than the cloud-filled RGB image. In frames 2 and 3, a bright-to-dark gradient tracks the continuous ground plane receding from ~1–2 m at the bottom edge to the distant background, reflecting the wearer's forward approach and head tilt, while confirming no other people or obstacles are present in front of the wearer. However, the depth map is unreliable for small ground objects and cross-frame scale consistency: the small ball resting on the grass (~3–5 m ahead on the lower-left in frame 2, approaching to ~1.5–2.5 m at the bottom-center in frame 3) merges completely into the surrounding ground surface, and frame 4's close-up ground (~0.5–1.5 m away) is rendered medium-grey rather than bright white due to per-frame normalization without a sky reference.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map is completely black across all five frames, detecting zero object or person instances throughout the sequence. While this accurately reflects the absence of any other people in the scene or visible body parts of the camera wearer (whose presence is only indicated by a shadow cast on the grass to the left in frame 4), it provides no spatial layout information beyond what is in the RGB strip. The map is unreliable for small and distant objects: it completely misses the small ball high in the air in frame 1 (~3–8 m above and in front of the wearer) and resting on the grass in frames 2 and 3 (moving from ~3–5 m away on the lower-left to ~1.5–2.5 m away near the bottom-center as the wearer approaches). It also fails to segment any background structures such as the perimeter fence, flagpole, and stadium light poles 40–80 m away along the field's edge.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand pose map is entirely black across all five frames, containing no yellow body skeletons or magenta hand skeletons. This confirms the spatial fact from the RGB strip that no other people are present anywhere on the field to face, look toward, or move relative to the camera wearer across the sequence. Furthermore, even when the camera wearer looks straight down at the grass within arm's reach (~0.5–1.5 m away) in frame 4 after approaching the ball from frames 2 to 3, the wearer's own hands, arms, and legs remain completely outside the camera's field of view (with only their shadow visible on the left). Because no human bodies or hands ever enter the frame, the pose map contributes no additional spatial cues beyond confirming an empty egocentric viewpoint.
